why: A country that never touches the levers panics about as often as the 19th century's large economies did.
Panics are sharp events, not a permanent state.
A panic lasts a season or two, as the historical ones did.
Manias are part of the century: about seven months in each ten years without a hand on the levers.
Many Manias end in a panic, as 1825, 1837, 1847, 1857, 1873 and 1890 did; the rest cool off.
A country that leaves the market alone still grows a little faster with it than without it.
Left alone, Bad Debts clear in a year or two.
More advanced finance brings more crashes late in the century, but never a world in constant crisis.
A hands-off country pays for the leverage it let build, as the long slump after 1873 did.
Confidence stays low for a while after a crash: the Wary tier is part of the cycle.
Good years are common but not the norm.
The Exchange is usually Respected or Trusted, and losing that means something.
Careful play pays, safely.
Even careful play meets a panic or two a century.
Careful play keeps the Exchange Respected or better almost all the time.
Running leverage up to 12 months and getting out pays better than careful play.
And no safe middle style makes the run-up pointless.
A player who goes for it reaches 12 months from time to time.
Most run-ups get out unscathed, and a good share do not.
The run-up is the riskier way to play.
High leverage is somewhere a player spends time.
The risk is real: in some worlds careful play does better.
A player riding leverage meets Manias.
Running up without watching the Panic Threshold is worth about what careful play is.
Reckless play throws the gains away.
AI countries use leverage, so rivals stay competitive.
AI countries panic about as history did, so Great Powers meet crises and the Long Depression can start.
AI countries have Manias too.
AI Exchanges are usually Respected or Trusted.
Some AI governments rescue their banks and some let the panic run.
